paper_a.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition (He et al., 2015)

metadata.description: Both introduce skip/shortcut connections to enable training of very deep networks. Highway networks use learned sigmoid gates to interpolate between transform and carry (identity); ResNet uses fixed identity shortcuts with additive residuals. ResNet can be viewed as a Highway network with gates fixed at T=0.5 (or equivalently T=1 with the residual absorbed). Concurrent work: Highway appeared ~6 months before ResNet.

matches.explanation: Both identify the same core problem: very deep networks are hard to train. ResNet frames this as the 'degradation problem' (higher training error with more layers); Highway frames it as vanishing/exploding gradients preventing SGD convergence. Same phenomenon, slightly different framings.

The central formulations. ResNet: $\mathbf{y} = \mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x}$ (learn residual, add identity). Highway: $\mathbf{y} = H(\mathbf{x}) \cdot T(\mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{x} \cdot (1 - T(\mathbf{x}))$ (gate-weighted interpolation). ResNet is the special case where $T = 1$ always (no gating), so the carry path always adds the full identity. The key design difference: ResNet's simplicity (no gate parameters) vs Highway's expressiveness (learned gates).
ResNet's projection shortcuts ($W_s \mathbf{x}$) for dimension changes have no direct counterpart in Highway networks, which typically assume matching dimensions or use zero-padding.

The learned transform gate $T(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_T \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{b}_T)$ is unique to Highway networks. ResNet deliberately avoids any gating mechanism, relying on the simpler additive identity shortcut. This is the fundamental architectural divergence.

Highway networks' 'information highway' concept and LSTM analogy are unique to that paper. ResNet does not draw on LSTM design; instead it motivates shortcuts from a function-approximation / residual-learning perspective.

Both make the same core claim: shortcut/gated connections enable training of very deep networks. ResNet argues that residual mappings are easier to optimize (pushing $\mathcal{F} \to 0$ is easier than learning identity). Highway argues that negative gate bias initializes near identity and lets optimization discover which layers to activate. Same conclusion, different theoretical justifications.

Both report CIFAR-10 results with deep networks (100+ layers for ResNet, 20-100 for Highway). ResNet achieves stronger results (6.43% with 110 layers) and scales to 1000+ layers. Highway networks demonstrate trainability but at somewhat lower accuracy levels.
ResNet's large-scale ImageNet results (3.57% top-5 ensemble error, ILSVRC 2015 winner) have no counterpart in the Highway paper, which focuses on smaller-scale experiments (MNIST, CIFAR).
ResNet's transfer to COCO detection (28% relative improvement) demonstrates backbone utility. Highway networks do not evaluate transfer learning.
Highway's MNIST experiment with up to 900 layers (demonstrating pure trainability) has no direct ResNet counterpart on MNIST, though ResNet's 1202-layer CIFAR-10 experiment serves a similar purpose.

ResNet's specific basic and bottleneck block architectures (designed for efficient scaling on ImageNet) have no counterpart in Highway networks, which use simpler fully-connected or thin convolutional layers.

Both use SGD training. The key difference: ResNet uses standard initialization (no special bias); Highway requires carefully initialized negative gate biases ($b_T = -1$ to $-3$) to start near identity. ResNet's identity shortcut achieves the same 'start near identity' effect without any initialization trick.
